subject: point survey for endemic bromeliad - questions on design

messages.author: e183a94721e02db4
messages.subject: point survey for endemic bromeliad - questions on design
parts:
Hi all,

I work for the department of environment in the Cayman Islands and we are attempting to estimate the population size and to create a distribution map of an endemic bromeliad in a restricted forest site. The site is ~ 55 acres and the plant is only found here plus a few small satellite lots around the main forest. We have chosen to use systematically placed points because of the jagged karst terrain found in the study area.

I have a few questions about the design:

The plants occur in singly and in cluster ranging from a few plants to ~15 plants. The clusters occur in tight bunches and larger plants have clonal vegetative growth. We are attempting to count the rosettes of the clusters so any large plant + its satellites. However, small single plants will still be counted. The cluster size is difficult to estimate correctly from a distance. Is it right to say that the detection function allows for this type of imperfect detection? 

I used the 'distance.sample.size' R package to estimate the sample size required for this survey. The estimated sample size ranges from 76 - 216 for a targeted CV = 15% depending on the dispersion parameter used (P was set to 0.5 but doesn't affect estimates in a large way).  The plant seems ubiquitous in the study area but also forms large clusters and is more abundant near wetlands. Because of its clustering pattern, I chose a dispersion parameter of 2 which results in a sample size of 120. The visibility in the forest and low and the truncation will most likely be in the range of 15 - 25 meters. This amount of coverage means that at w = 15  we cover 39% of the study area and at w= 25 we cover 105%. Is there a recommended proportion coverage for a plant and study area like this? If I use the more conservative estimate of 74 (dispersion parameter = 1) the proportion covered seems more reasonable with 23% covered at w=15 and 65% at w = 25. 

I went out and did two random points and obtained 26 detections which produced the attached detection function. With more samples I expect the detection function to fill out but I think 25m will be near the maximum observable distance. I have also attached some images of plant clusters for reference. Plus, I attached an image of the survey site and 120 survey points.




Any answers or comments will be useful. We are going to do another pilot on Friday to better inform the sampling strategy. 

References:
Clark, R.G., 2016. Statistical efficiency in distance sampling. PloS one, 11(3).

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: {Disarmed} Re: [distance-sampling] point survey for endemic bromeliad - questions on design
parts:
Vaughn

Several brief thoughts.  I presume the clearings within the forest are not to be considered part of your study area as you seem to intentionally avoid placing survey effort within them; is that correct?

I appreciate it may be difficult to count individuals in a cluster from the point.  However, distance sampling permits the recording of detections from the point station, then confirmation of the group size could be made by walking up to the group for closer examination.  Marine mammal researchers do this regularly by breaking from their survey transects to steam toward a group of cetaceans to obtain a better estimate of group size.  There are many forms of uncertainty in surveys that are outside your control, in this situation, uncertainty in estimation of group size in within your means to control.

Regarding the proportion of the study area that should be surveyed; there is no rigid guidance on this matter.  Going back to the analogy of marine cetacean surveys: in the remote Southern Ocean it can be prohibitive to survey much more than 1% of the study area.  Nevertheless, defensible estimates can be produced.  At the other extreme, having point stations with detection radii that overlap (your w=25 situation) where the covered region exceeds the size of the study area; can be considered problematic because of potential double counting.  However, a simulation investigation of this by Buckland (2006) suggested the overlap issue did not induce large bias.

The question of sample size in distance sampling surveys boils down to two questions: a) are there sufficient detections to properly characterise the shape of the detection function and thereby reliably estimate the probability of detecting objects within the truncation distance and b) is there adequate spatial replication of samplers (lines or points) within the study area to accurately characterise the variability in encounter rate between samplers.

If you were to follow the sample size recommendations in Buckland et al. (2015) Section MailScanner warning: numerical links are often malicious: 2.4.2.1 (also available in the lecture notes on sample size considerations in our online workshop materials (https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/lecturepdfs/Ch4/L4-3%20Sample%20Size.pdf) the number of stations needed (based upon your pilot study with 26 detections from 2 stations) is on the order of 10 stations.

References

Buckland, S. T. 2006. ‘Point Transect Surveys for Songbirds: Robust Methodologies’. The Auk 123 (2): 345–345. https://doi.org/10.1642/0004-8038(2006)123[345:psfsrm]2.0.co;2.

Buckland, S.T., E. Rexstad, T.A. Marques and C.S. Oedekoven. 2015. Distance Sampling: Methods and Applications. Springer.

messages.author: e183a94721e02db4
messages.subject: Re: {Disarmed} Re: [distance-sampling] point survey for endemic bromeliad - questions on design
parts:
Hi Eric,

Thanks for the quick response!

Yes, the cleared areas are wetlands within the study area that we will not be surveying in.

Ok, that is good to know. We will estimate cluster size from the point, record the actual cluster size when we measure each distance, and then compare estimates from both counts. In the pilot run, I consistently underestimated the cluster size. A challenge will be in situations where we want to bin a distance because of dangerous terrain and/or difficult vegetation to cross where getting exact distances or exact cluster size will take a lot of effort. But I guess having a mixed bag of exact and non-exact counts will be less biased than using purely non-exact counts.


Thanks for the references. I am confident that we will have a sufficient number of detections with a fairly small sample size but the encounter variance between samplers is hard to predict. My pilot may have been in two high-density locations and could be misleading. I will aim for a sample size of around 50 points which at w = 25 m will cover ~ 45% of the survey area. I'm going higher than 10 samplers because of the uncertainty in encounter variance and because I would like a sufficient number of points to keep the spatial variance low for the distribution model.

I also just noticed the new R package 'dssm' that the distance sampling team have created.. it looks great!!  

Thanks for the advice.

Vaughn
